text: The Bone Wars were a bitter race between two American [[fossil|fossil]] hunters, Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, in the late 1800s. Each wanted to find and name more new animals than the other.

They hired teams to dig across the American West, bribed each other's workers, spread rumours and attacked each other in print. Sometimes their teams even destroyed fossils so the other side could not have them. Yet the race also produced some of the most famous dinosaurs ever named, including [[@triceratops-horns|Triceratops]] and [[@stegosaurus|Stegosaurus]].

He gave it legs instead of flippers
He made it ten times too big

st.reveal: Cope thought the long part was the tail and attached the skull to the wrong end. The error was pointed out, and Marsh never let him forget it. Cope tried to buy up every copy of the paper with the mistake.

myth: Brontosaurus was a hoax made by putting the wrong head on a skeleton.

The skeleton was real. No head had been found with it, so museums mounted it with a borrowed skull from a different long-necked dinosaur. The body was genuine, and many scientists again treat Brontosaurus as a real, separate animal.
facts: Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh

sec.t:
Cope and Marsh met in Germany in 1864 and at first got on well. They even named fossils after each other. Marsh worked at Yale University and had a rich uncle, the banker George Peabody, who paid for Yale's natural history museum. Cope was a brilliant but hot-tempered scientist from a wealthy [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|Philadelphia]] family.

At that time, very few dinosaurs were known in North America. The best was Hadrosaurus, a duck-billed plant-eater dug up in New Jersey in 1858. It had been described by Joseph Leidy, a careful Philadelphia scientist who had helped train Cope. Leidy later grew tired of the fighting and turned to other kinds of science.

Things went sour in the late 1860s. Cope described a long-necked [[@ocean-reptiles|sea reptile]] called Elasmosaurus, but put its head on the end of its tail. The mistake was pointed out publicly. Soon after, Marsh paid workers at a quarry Cope was using to send the best fossils to him instead.

Speed mattered most, because the first published name wins. Cope sometimes sent descriptions to journals by telegram. Both men named animals from just a few bones, and sometimes named the same animal twice. That rush caused muddles that took scientists decades to sort out, including the long confusion over [[@dino-names|Brontosaurus]].

In 1890, the feud spilled into the New York Herald, a popular [[@news-media|newspaper]]. Cope accused Marsh of stealing ideas and mismanaging government money. Marsh fired back. Readers enjoyed the scandal, but it damaged the reputation of both men.

By the end, Marsh had named about 80 new kinds of dinosaur and Cope about 56. Many are still accepted. Marsh named Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Allosaurus and Diplodocus. Cope named Camarasaurus and Coelophysis, among many other fossil animals.

The rivalry ruined them both. Cope lost much of his fortune in bad investments, and Marsh lost his government funding. Cope died in 1897 and Marsh in 1899. Their fossils still fill the great halls of museums in New York, New Haven, Washington and Philadelphia. Some crates of their bones sat unopened for many years after they died.

text: Moa were giant flightless birds that lived only in [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]]. There were nine kinds. The biggest, the South Island giant moa, could reach about 3.6 metres tall with its neck stretched up, taller than a basketball hoop. It could weigh about 230 kg, as much as a grand piano.

Moa ate leaves, twigs, seeds and fruit, and filled the role that deer or antelope play on other continents. They lived for millions of years. But within roughly 200 years of people arriving in New Zealand, around 1300 CE, they were all gone.

st.prompt: Moa could not fly. Which bird, alive today, turned out to be one of their closest relatives?

options.t: The tinamou, a small bird of South America that can fly
The kiwi of New Zealand
The ostrich of Africa

st.reveal: DNA from moa bones showed that their closest living relatives are tinamous, chicken-sized birds that can fly short distances. This suggests the moa's ancestors flew to New Zealand and later lost their wings.

Mitchell, K. et al. (2014), Ancient DNA reveals elephant birds and kiwi are sister taxa, Science.
n.certNote: Moa bones and DNA tell us a lot about their size and family tree. The exact date of their extinction and the size of their population are still estimated.

sec.t:
Many birds can't fly, like ostriches, emus and penguins. But they all still have wings, even if they're tiny. Moa had none. Their skeletons show no wing bones at all.

That's unusual among birds. Scientists think moa lost their wings because they had no need for them. New Zealand had no land [[mammal|mammals]] hunting on the ground, apart from bats. Birds could walk, nest and feed safely, so many of them became flightless.

In the largest kinds of moa, the females were much bigger than the males. Females could be about 1.5 times taller and nearly three times heavier.

For years, scientists thought the big and small moa bones belonged to different [[species|species]]. [[dna|DNA]] tests in the early 2000s showed they were the same species, just mothers and fathers. Big females probably ruled their patches of forest.

Moa eggs were huge too. Some were around 24 cm long, much bigger than a coconut. Their shells were thin, so scientists think lighter males may have sat on them.

{{story:polynesians}}

The moa had one big enemy before people arrived: Haast's eagle. It was the largest eagle known, with a wingspan of up to about 3 metres and talons as large as a tiger's claws.

Like [[@eagles-hunt|other eagles]], it relied on speed and surprise. It hunted moa by swooping down, grabbing the bird's back or neck and striking hard. When moa disappeared, the eagle lost its main food, and it died out too. Māori stories may remember it as a giant bird called Pouakai or Te Hōkioi.

Polynesian voyagers, ancestors of the Māori, sailed to New Zealand around 1300 CE in great canoes. They were some of the greatest [[@polynesians|navigators]] in history, finding islands across thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

They found a land full of large, slow-breeding birds that had never seen humans. Moa were hunted for meat, their bones were carved into tools and jewellery, and their eggshells were used as water containers. Forests were also burned to clear land.

Moa laid only one or two eggs at a time and took years to grow up. So hunting even a small number each year was enough to tip them towards extinction. By about 1400 to 1450, they were gone.

sec.h: What we know from their remains
sec.t:
Moa left plenty behind. Scientists have found complete skeletons, eggs, feathers and even dried muscle and skin in caves. Their gizzard stones, swallowed to grind tough plants, have been found in piles.

Ancient DNA from moa bones has revealed their family tree. Surprisingly, their closest living relatives are tinamous, small birds from South America that can fly. That means the moa's ancestors probably flew to New Zealand millions of years ago, then grew big and lost their wings.

In July 2025, the American company Colossal Biosciences announced a project to try to bring back the moa. It is working with the Ngāi Tahu Research Centre, linked to a South Island Māori tribe, and the film director Peter Jackson.

Many scientists are doubtful. A "new" moa would be a modern bird with some moa [[gene|genes]], not the real thing, and it's unclear where it would live. Some argue the money would be better spent saving living birds, like New Zealand's [[endangered|endangered]] kākāpō. The moa's story sits alongside the [[@dodo|dodo]] as one of the clearest warnings about how quickly people can wipe out an animal.

text: The two Voyager space probes are the most distant human-made objects. Voyager 1 is more than 25 billion km from Earth, about 170 times farther than Earth is from the Sun. Voyager 2 is more than 21 billion km away. Both are still travelling outward at around 55,000 to 61,000 km/h, and both are still sending messages home.

They were launched in 1977 to visit the giant planets. After that job was done, they kept going. Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space, the space between the stars, in 2012. Voyager 2 followed in 2018.

st.prompt: How long does a radio message from Earth take to reach Voyager 1?

options.t: Almost a whole day
About one second
About a year

st.reveal: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km every second. Even so, Voyager 1 is so far away that a command takes nearly 24 hours to arrive, and the reply takes another day to come back.

NASA, The Golden Record.
n.certNote: Both Voyagers have left the Sun's bubble of solar wind and entered interstellar space. Whether that counts as "leaving the solar system" depends on how you define the solar system's edge.

myth: The Voyagers have left the solar system completely.

They have passed out of the Sun's bubble of solar wind into interstellar space. But the Sun's gravity still holds a vast cloud of icy objects much farther out, and it will take the Voyagers tens of thousands of years to get beyond it.
facts: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (Voyager 2 all four)

sec.t:
In the late 1970s, [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]], Saturn, Uranus and Neptune were lined up in a way that happens only about once every 176 years. A spacecraft could swing past one planet and use its [[gravity|gravity]] to fling it on to the next, like a slingshot. NASA took the chance.

Voyager 2 launched first, on 20 August 1977. Voyager 1 followed on 5 September, on a faster path, so it overtook its twin. Each probe weighed about 800 kg, about the weight of a small car.

Both Voyagers flew past Jupiter in 1979. They showed its Great Red Spot up close and discovered [[@volcano|volcanoes]] erupting on its [[@space-weird-volcano-moon|moon Io]], the first active volcanoes seen beyond Earth. Both then visited Saturn. Voyager 1 swung close to Saturn's giant moon [[@titan|Titan]], which bent its path up and out of the plane of the planets.

Voyager 2 carried on. It reached [[@uranus-sideways|Uranus]] in 1986 and [[@neptune-winds|Neptune]] in 1989. It is still the only spacecraft to have visited either planet. Almost everything we know about them up close comes from those brief flybys.

On 14 February 1990, Voyager 1 turned its camera back towards home. From about 6 billion km away, Earth appeared as a tiny speck, less than a single [[pixel|pixel]], in a beam of sunlight. The [[astronomer|astronomer]] Carl Sagan called it the [[@space-first-photo-earth|Pale Blue Dot]].

Each Voyager carries a [[@space-golden-record|golden record]], a gold-plated copper disc 30 cm wide, with a needle and pictures showing how to play it. It holds greetings in 55 languages, sounds of Earth such as rain, birds and a mother's kiss, and 90 minutes of music from around the world.

One track is "Jaat Kahan Ho", a song in [[raga|raga]] Bhairavi sung by the Hindustani classical singer Kesarbai Kerkar. Listen to more about [[@carnatic-hindustani|Hindustani and Carnatic music]]. Other tracks include Bach, [[@beethoven|Beethoven]], and Chuck Berry's [[@rock-music|rock and roll]] song "Johnny B. Goode".

{{story:carnatic-hindustani}}

The chance that anyone finds a record is tiny. Its makers saw it as a message about who we are as much as a letter to [[@space-aliens-look|aliens]].

The Voyagers run on electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium. That power drops a little every year, so engineers have switched off heaters and instruments one by one to keep the most important ones working.

Their transmitters are about as strong as a fridge light bulb. By the time the signal reaches Earth, it is billions of times weaker than the power of a watch battery. NASA's Deep Space Network catches it with giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia.

In late 2023, Voyager 1 began sending back gibberish. Engineers traced the problem to a single failed memory chip. Working with computer code written in the 1970s, they moved the affected instructions to other parts of its memory. By April 2024, Voyager 1 was sending sensible data again.

NASA expects the Voyagers to run out of power for any instrument some time in the 2030s. After that, they will drift silently on. In about 40,000 years, Voyager 1 will pass within about 1.6 [[@light-years|light-years]] of a small star called Gliese 445. Even then, it will have crossed only a tiny fraction of our [[galaxy|galaxy]].

text: The Indian Air Force protects India's skies. Its pilots fly fighter jets that can intercept unknown aircraft, and it runs radars that watch the airspace day and night. In a war, it supports the army on the ground and the navy at sea.

It also does a great deal of work that has nothing to do with fighting. Its [[@helicopters|helicopters]] rescue people from floods and landslides. Its giant transport planes fly supplies to soldiers on snowy mountain posts, carry aid to other countries after disasters, and bring Indians home from war zones. It was founded on 8 October 1932, which is why Air Force Day is celebrated every 8 October.

Most of the time, the Indian Air Force is training, guarding the skies and helping in emergencies. It has carried food and medicine after cyclones and floods, rescued pilgrims in the mountains and flown Indians home from conflict zones abroad.

sec.t:
The Air Force began very small. Its first flight, formed in 1933, had a handful of Westland Wapiti biplanes, two-winged planes with open cockpits. During the Second World War it grew quickly and was given the title "Royal". When India became a [[republic|republic]] in 1950, the "Royal" was dropped.

Since then it has flown many kinds of aircraft. The MiG-21, a fast Soviet-designed jet, served for more than 60 years before its final flight in September 2025. Today the fighters include the Russian-designed Su-30MKI, the French Rafale and the Tejas, a light jet designed and built in India. The Air Force also flies large transport planes such as the C-17 Globemaster and C-130J, and helicopters including the Dhruv and the Prachand, both made in India by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.

India has some of the hardest flying conditions anywhere. In Ladakh, the airstrip at Daulat Beg Oldi sits about 5,000 metres above sea level. Air that high is thin, so wings make less lift and engines produce less power. Landing a big plane there takes careful skill.

Helicopters fly supplies to soldiers on the Siachen Glacier, among the highest places where people are posted all year round. Pilots must deal with sudden storms, icy winds and narrow valleys. Knowing [[@airplanes-fly|how planes fly]] in thin air is a matter of life and death there.

In 1984, Squadron Leader Rakesh Sharma, an Air Force pilot, flew on a Soviet spacecraft and became the first Indian in space. In June 2025, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla, another Air Force pilot, flew to the International Space Station. Several of India's [[@indian-astronauts|astronauts]] for the Gaganyaan programme also come from the Air Force, because test pilots are trained to stay calm when things go wrong.

Women have flown Air Force helicopters and transport planes since the 1990s. In 2016, Avani Chaturvedi, Bhawana Kanth and Mohana Singh were commissioned as India's first women fighter pilots. Today women fly fighter jets in front-line squadrons, and women officers serve across the force as engineers, air traffic controllers and meteorologists.

On Air Force Day, crowds gather to watch the Surya Kiran team fly red-and-white jets just a few metres apart, and the Sarang team swing their helicopters around each other like dancers. Behind the show are years of training.

text: A crab's skeleton is on the outside, a hard shell called an [[@exoskeletons|exoskeleton]]. It protects the crab well, but it can't stretch. So to grow, a crab has to moult.

First it builds a new, soft, wrinkled shell underneath the old one. Then the old shell cracks open along the back, and the crab slowly backs out of it. It swallows water to puff up its soft body, so the new shell will set larger than the last. For a few days, the crab is soft and helpless and stays hidden. As the new shell hardens, the crab grows into the extra space. Then the whole cycle starts again.

st.reveal: A freshly moulted crab takes in water to swell its soft body so the new shell sets bigger than the old one. For several days it is soft and defenceless, so it hides. Later it replaces the water with new tissue as it grows into its roomier armour.

sec.t:
Moulting is risky and exhausting. Weeks before, the crab starts taking some calcium back out of its old shell to save it. A new soft skin forms beneath.

When it's time, the crab pumps itself up with water until the old shell splits at the back. It then pulls out every part of its body, including each leg, each claw and the stalks of its eyes. The thin lining of its gills and the hard grinding teeth inside its stomach come away too. The whole thing can take minutes or hours, and a crab that gets stuck may die.

Afterwards, many crabs eat their old shell to get back the minerals in it. Nothing useful goes to waste.

Crabs start life as tiny drifting [[larva|larvae]] that look nothing like crabs. They float in the sea as part of the [[plankton|plankton]] and moult again and again, changing shape each time. Eventually they settle on the seabed as miniature crabs.

Young crabs may moult every few weeks. Older ones slow down, moulting once a year or less, and some stop entirely. A crab that loses a leg in a fight, or drops it on purpose to escape a [[predator|predator]], can regrow it, a little bigger with each moult.

Size varies enormously. The Japanese spider crab has legs that can span about 3.7 m, as wide as a small car is long. The coconut crab, which lives on islands in the Indian and Pacific oceans, including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, can weigh about 4 kg and crack coconuts with its claws.

Hermit crabs never grow a full hard shell. Their soft, curly back end needs protection, so they live in empty snail shells. When a hermit crab outgrows one, it looks for a bigger one. Sometimes several crabs line up from largest to smallest by a new shell, and each moves up one size in turn.

On [[@beaches|beaches]] in Goa, Odisha and Chennai, pale ghost crabs dart sideways at high speed and vanish into holes. In mudflats and [[lagoon|lagoons]] like [[@chilika|Chilika]], male fiddler crabs wave one giant claw to attract mates. And on Christmas Island, an Australian [[territory|territory]] in the Indian Ocean, tens of millions of red crabs march from the forest to the sea each year to breed. Roads close and bridges are built just for them, one of the great [[@animal-migration-land|animal migrations]] on land.

text: The ocean is very noisy, but our ears are not built to hear it from above the surface. Sound travels through water about four times faster than through air, and it can go a long way. Waves crash, rain patters, ice cracks and underwater earthquakes rumble. On top of that, animals use [[@sound-travel|sound]] to find food, find each other and stay safe.

Whales sing, dolphins click and whistle, fish grunt and drum, and tiny shrimp crackle like bacon frying in a pan. Scientists listen with [[@microphones|underwater microphones]] called [[hydrophone|hydrophones]]. Since the 1900s, ships have added their own constant hum of engines and [[propeller|propellers]].

st.prompt: Sound travels through air at about 340 m per second. How fast does it travel through seawater?

About 340 m per second, the same

st.reveal: Water is far denser and harder to squeeze than air, so vibrations pass through it faster. Sound in seawater travels at about 1,500 m per second. That is why whales can hear each other across huge distances.

myth: The ocean is a silent world.

A famous 1956 film about the sea was even called "The Silent World". In fact, the ocean is full of sound, from waves, rain, cracking ice and earthquakes to animals clicking, singing, grunting and drumming.
facts: lets some sounds travel thousands of km

sec.t:
Underwater, light fades fast. Below about 200 m, it is dim, and below 1,000 m there is no sunlight at all. Sound behaves differently. It can travel for tens or even thousands of kilometres.

That is why so many sea animals rely on it. Dolphins and toothed whales use [[@echolocation|echolocation]], sending out clicks and listening for the echoes, to find fish in murky or dark water. Humpback whales sing long, repeating songs that can last for hours. The deep calls of blue whales are some of the [[@extreme-loudest-animals|loudest sounds]] made by any animal, and are low enough that many people couldn't hear them even if they were there.

About 1 km down in many parts of the ocean, there is a layer where sound gets trapped and bounces along like light in a glass fibre. Scientists call it the SOFAR channel. Sound in this layer can travel across a whole ocean. During the Second World War, the American scientist Maurice Ewing showed that a small explosion set off in the channel could be heard thousands of kilometres away. Navies saw at once how useful that could be.

The US Navy built networks of hydrophones to listen for [[@submarines|submarines]]. They also picked up strange sounds. In 1997, scientists at NOAA recorded a deep, rising noise in the South Pacific that they called "[[@mystery-bloop|the Bloop]]". Rumours spread about a giant unknown creature. Years later, they concluded it was probably ice cracking and breaking off from Antarctica.

Ships, sonar, oil and gas surveys and building work at sea all add sound to the ocean. Large ships make a low rumble that overlaps with the calls of big whales. Scientists worry that this noise can make it harder for whales to hear each other, a bit like trying to talk at a loud wedding.

When shipping slowed down during the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, researchers in several places noticed the sea had become quieter. That gave them a rare chance to compare. Some ports and shipping lanes now ask ships to slow down near whale areas, which makes them quieter and safer for [[@whale-songs|whales]] at the same time.

text: The "lead" in a pencil is graphite, a soft, grey form of carbon, mixed with clay. It is made into long, thin rods and baked hard in an oven. Then the rods are laid in grooves cut into a flat strip of wood. A second grooved strip is glued on top, like a sandwich, and the whole thing is cut into pencils.

So nobody pushes the core into a hole. The pencil is built around it. The shape is cut, the outside is painted, and the end might get a metal band and an eraser. A big factory can make hundreds of thousands of pencils a day.

st.reveal: Factories cut grooves into a flat slat of wood, lay the cores in them, glue a second grooved slat on top and then slice the sandwich into separate pencils. Drilling a hole that long and thin would be almost impossible.

sec.t:
When people first found graphite, they thought it was a kind of lead, because both are grey and leave a mark. They called it "black lead" or "plumbago". The name stuck, even after chemists showed in the 1700s that graphite is carbon.

The first big find was at Borrowdale, in the hills of north-west England, in the 1500s. The graphite there was so pure it could be sawn into sticks and used for writing. Shepherds used it to mark their sheep. Before that, people had written with [[@writing-tools|tools]] like reed pens, quills and sticks of soft metal. Because it was so valuable, the mine was guarded, and stealing graphite became a serious crime.

Graphite is made of flat sheets of carbon [[atom|atoms]] stacked on top of each other, like a deck of cards. The sheets slide apart very easily. When you drag a pencil across paper, the rough paper scrapes off flakes, which stick in its fibres and leave a grey line.

That's also why pencil marks can be rubbed out. The graphite sits on top of the paper instead of soaking in like ink, so an [[@erasers|eraser]] can lift it off.

Diamond is carbon too, with its atoms locked in a rigid 3D pattern, which makes it the hardest natural material. Graphite and diamond are made of the same [[element|element]], arranged differently. In factories, graphite squeezed under enormous heat and pressure can even be turned into small diamonds.

Pencil makers need wood that is soft enough to sharpen easily but doesn't splinter. In the US, incense cedar from California is popular. In India, most pencil wood is poplar, and much of it comes from the [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] Valley. Around Pulwama, many villages grow poplar trees for pencil factories.

Once glued and cut, pencils get several coats of paint. Many American pencils are yellow. In the 1890s, a company called Koh-i-Noor started selling fancy yellow pencils, and yellow came to suggest quality. Others copied the colour.

There's a story that NASA spent millions on a space pen while Russian cosmonauts just used pencils. It isn't really true. Both used pencils at first. But pencil tips can snap off, and tiny flakes of graphite floating in a spacecraft could get into electronics, so both countries later switched to special pens made by a private company.

text: Most solar panels are made of thin slices of silicon, a material made from purified sand. Each panel holds dozens of these slices, called solar cells. Every cell has two layers of silicon, treated with tiny amounts of other [[element|elements]] so that one layer has spare [[electron|electrons]] and the other has gaps where electrons are missing. Where the two layers meet, an invisible electric "slope" forms.

When sunlight hits the cell, its energy knocks electrons loose from silicon [[atom|atoms]]. The slope pushes those free electrons one way, towards a metal contact on top. Connect a wire from the top to the bottom, and the electrons flow round it as an electric current. No moving parts, no fuel and no noise: just light going in and electricity coming out.

sec.t:
The first big customers were satellites, which could not carry enough fuel for years in [[orbit|orbit]]. In 1958, the USA launched Vanguard 1, a satellite the size of a grapefruit, with small solar cells on its outside. Its radio fell silent in 1964, but the satellite is still up there. It is the oldest human-made object in orbit around Earth.

Today almost every [[@satellites-help|satellite]], the International [[@space-station|Space Station]] and many of India's [[@india-space-budget|ISRO]] spacecraft run on sunlight caught by large solar wings.

India gets plenty of strong sunshine, and solar power has grown very fast there since the 2010s. The Bhadla Solar Park in the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]] of Rajasthan is one of the largest in the world. Its rows of panels cover about 57 square kilometres, roughly the area of 8,000 football fields. In 2015, Cochin International Airport in Kerala became the first airport in the world to run entirely on solar power.

Rooftop panels now sit on homes, schools and railway stations across India and the USA. Because the panels make electricity right where it is used, less is wasted travelling long distances through wires.

Panels make no electricity at night and less on cloudy or dusty days. In Rajasthan's deserts, workers and robots clean dust off the panels regularly, because a layer of dust can block a lot of light. To keep the lights on after sunset, solar power is often paired with [[@batteries|batteries]] or other power stations.

The best panels sold today turn just over a fifth of the sunlight hitting them into electricity. A leaf does far worse, storing only about 1% of sunlight through [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. The leaf, though, builds and repairs itself for free.

यह कला अक्सर एक साथ मज़ेदार भी होती है और चुभने वाली भी। एक चूहा तख़्ती पकड़े खड़ा है। एक लड़की दिल के आकार के लाल गुब्बारे की ओर हाथ बढ़ा रही है। पुलिसवाले तकियों से लड़ रहे हैं। बहुत-सी तस्वीरें युद्ध, पैसे या ताकतवर लोगों का मज़ाक उड़ाती हैं। बैंक्सी का काम ब्रिटेन से दूर भी दिखा है, न्यूयॉर्क, पेरिस और वेस्ट बैंक की दीवारों पर, और 2022 में यूक्रेन की बमबारी से टूटी इमारतों पर। बैंक्सी ने 1990 के दशक में शुरुआत की, शायद पश्चिमी इंग्लैंड के ब्रिस्टल में, और 2000 के दशक तक वह दुनिया के सबसे जाने-माने जीवित कलाकारों में गिना जाने लगा।

sec.t:
अक्टूबर 2018 में [[@london|लंदन]] के एक नीलामीघर में गर्ल विद बलून की एक फ़्रेम की हुई प्रति दस लाख पाउंड से थोड़ा ज़्यादा में बिकी (पाउंड ब्रिटेन की [[currency|मुद्रा]] है)। जैसे ही हथौड़ा गिरा, एक अलार्म बजा और कैनवस फ़्रेम के नीचे से सरकने लगा, एक छिपे श्रेडर से पट्टियों में कटते हुए।

पूरे कमरे की साँस अटक गई। बैंक्सी ने एक वीडियो डाला, जिसमें दिखाया गया कि बरसों पहले फ़्रेम में श्रेडर लगाया गया था। वह आधे रास्ते में अटक गया, और लड़की का निचला आधा हिस्सा फीतों की तरह लटकता रह गया। खरीदार ने उसे रखने का फ़ैसला किया। तीन साल बाद वही आधी कटी कृति फिर बिकी, लगभग 1.86 करोड़ पाउंड में। कला बाज़ार का मज़ाक उड़ाने के लिए किए गए एक करतब ने कला को कहीं ज़्यादा कीमती बना दिया।

sec.h: दीवारें जो अचानक कीमती हो जाती हैं
sec.t:
जब कोई नया बैंक्सी दिखता है, तो अजीब बातें होती हैं। मालिकों ने रंग बचाने के लिए दीवारों पर पारदर्शी प्लास्टिक लगा दिया है। कुछ ने ईंटों का पूरा हिस्सा काटकर बेच दिया है। जो नगर परिषदें आम तौर पर ग्रैफ़िटी रगड़कर मिटा देती हैं, वे बहस में पड़ गई हैं कि इसे रखें या नहीं।

2009 में ब्रिस्टल के शहर संग्रहालय में बैंक्सी की एक अचानक प्रदर्शनी लगी, जो चुपके से तैयार की गई थी। लगभग तीन महीनों में 3,00,000 से ज़्यादा लोग उसे देखने आए, कुछ बाहर घंटों कतार में खड़े रहे।

अगस्त 2024 में नौ दिनों तक हर दिन लंदन में कहीं न कहीं एक नया जानवर दिखा। एक दीवार पर बकरी, एक पुल पर बंदर, एक कार पर चढ़ता गैंडा और लंदन चिड़ियाघर में एक गोरिल्ला। कुछ ही घंटों में भीड़ जुट गई। कुछ कृतियाँ लगभग उतनी ही जल्दी खराब कर दी गईं या उठा ली गईं।

यह [[ethics|नैतिकता]] का सवाल है, और लोग आज भी एकमत नहीं हैं। कुछ बैंक्सी को एक बहादुर कलाकार मानते हैं जो आम गलियों तक कला लाता है, जहाँ कोई भी आम [[citizen|नागरिक]] उसे मुफ़्त देख सकता है। दूसरे याद दिलाते हैं कि ज़्यादातर ग्रैफ़िटी कलाकारों पर इसी काम के लिए जुर्माना लगता है, और किसी मशहूर नाम से नियम नहीं बदलने चाहिए।

बैंक्सी ने बड़े प्रोजेक्ट भी किए हैं, जैसे 2015 में डिस्मालैंड, अंग्रेज़ी समुद्र तट पर एक उदास नकली थीम पार्क, जो हँसते-खेलते परिवारों वाले थीम पार्कों का मज़ाक उड़ाता था। उसके ज़्यादातर काम की तरह, इसने भी लोगों से पहले हँसने और फिर सोचने को कहा। [[@famous-paintings|मशहूर पेंटिंगें]] सहेजने वाले संग्रहालय अब बैंक्सी पर भी बहस करते हैं, जो सड़क से शुरुआत करने वाले कलाकार के लिए शायद सबसे अनोखा मोड़ है।

text: स्टंट कलाकार योजना, अभ्यास और चतुर साधनों से सुरक्षित रहते हैं। किसी बड़े स्टंट से पहले एक टीम हर कदम का हिसाब लगाती है: दूरियाँ, रफ़्तार, गिरने की जगहें और क्या-क्या गड़बड़ हो सकती है। फिर वे अभ्यास करते हैं, अक्सर कई बार, धीमी रफ़्तार से शुरू करके।

शूटिंग के दिन वे छिपे हुए सहारों का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जैसे एयरबैग, गद्दे, तार, हार्नेस और टूटने के लिए बनी चीज़ें। कैमरे ऐसी जगह रखे जाते हैं कि छोटी-सी छलाँग विशाल लगे, या बाल-बाल बचा वार असली चोट लगे। फिर कंप्यूटर सुरक्षा का सामान मिटा देते हैं। सबसे अच्छे स्टंट परदे पर ख़तरनाक दिखते हैं, पर पूरी तरह काबू में होते हैं।

हर स्टंट एक स्टंट कोऑर्डिनेटर चलाता है। वही एक्शन रचता है, कलाकार चुनता है, सामान जाँचता है, और अगर कुछ भी असुरक्षित लगे तो शूटिंग रोकने का अधिकार रखता है।

बहुत-से स्टंट कलाकार जिमनास्टिक, युद्ध-कलाओं, गोताखोरी या घुड़सवारी जैसे खेलों से आते हैं। वे बिना चोट खाए गिरना, लुढ़कना और नकली घूँसा खाना सीखते हैं। सबसे जोखिम भरे दृश्य अक्सर हीरो जैसा दिखने वाला स्टंट डबल करता है।

अब तक के सबसे मशहूर स्टंटों में से एक 1928 में मूक फ़िल्म *स्टीमबोट बिल, जूनियर* में हुआ। लगभग दो टन वज़नी एक घर की सामने वाली दीवार अभिनेता बस्टर कीटन की ओर गिरी।

वे ठीक उस जगह खड़े थे जहाँ ऊपर के कमरे की एक खुली खिड़की आकर गिरनी थी। खिड़की का चौखटा उनके चारों ओर से निकल गया, दोनों तरफ़ बस कुछ सेंटीमीटर की जगह छोड़कर। अगर वे ज़रा भी इधर-उधर खड़े होते, तो कुचल जाते। आज कोई फ़िल्म ऐसा ख़तरा नहीं उठाने देगी। आज की टीमें पुतलों, हल्के सेटों और कंप्यूटर इफ़ेक्ट से परख करतीं।

आग वाले दृश्यों के लिए कलाकार पोशाक के नीचे आग-रोधी सूट पहनते हैं और खुली त्वचा पर एक ठंडा बचाव वाला जेल लगाते हैं। अग्निशामक लिए सुरक्षा टीमें कैमरे से ज़रा हटकर खड़ी रहती हैं।

लड़ाइयों में खिड़कियाँ और बोतलें ब्रेकअवे सामग्री से बनती हैं। कभी टीमें उबली हुई चीनी इस्तेमाल करती थीं, जो काँच जैसी दिखती और आसानी से भुरभुरा जाती थी। आज ज़्यादातर हल्की रेज़िन से बनती हैं, जो भोथरे टुकड़ों में टूटती है।

तार और हार्नेस कलाकारों को उड़ने, इमारतों के बीच छलाँग लगाने या कमरे में उछलकर फेंके जाने देते हैं। तारों को आसपास के रंग में रँग दिया जाता है, या बाद में कंप्यूटर पर मिटा दिया जाता है। बहुत-से सुपरहीरो दृश्यों में असली तारों का काम और [[@special-effects|स्पेशल इफ़ेक्ट]] मिले होते हैं।

भारत का अपना लंबा स्टंट इतिहास है। 1930 के दशक में फ़ियरलेस नाडिया नाम से मशहूर एक अभिनेत्री अपने स्टंट खुद करके सितारा बन गईं। 1935 की फ़िल्म *हंटरवाली* में उन्होंने कोड़े फटकारे, झूमरों से झूलीं और खलनायकों से लड़ीं, जो उस ज़माने में परदे पर किसी औरत के लिए दुर्लभ बात थी।

आज [[@bollywood|बॉलीवुड]] और दक्षिण भारतीय फ़िल्म उद्योग एक्शन निर्देशकों और स्टंटमैनों की बड़ी टीमें रखते हैं। कार का पीछा, मोटरसाइकिल की छलाँगें और लड़ाई के दृश्य अक्सर दुनिया भर के माहिरों के साथ फ़िल्माए जाते हैं।

दशकों तक स्टंट कलाकार शिकायत करते रहे कि अकादमी अवॉर्ड में उनके काम का कोई इनाम नहीं। अप्रैल 2025 में अकादमी ने स्टंट डिज़ाइन के एक नए ऑस्कर की घोषणा की। यह पहली बार 2028 में, 100वें अकादमी अवॉर्ड में दिया जाएगा।

फिर भी सबसे अच्छे स्टंट अक्सर वे होते हैं जिन पर तुम्हारा ध्यान ही नहीं जाता। एक अच्छा गिरना इसलिए आसान दिखता है क्योंकि उसके पीछे हफ़्तों की वह मेहनत है जो तुम कभी नहीं देखते, और वह छिपी मेहनत [[@behind-film-making|फ़िल्म कैसे बनती है]] की कहानी का एक छोटा-सा हिस्सा है।

text: इंप्रेशनिज़्म चित्रकारी की एक शैली है जो 1860 और 1870 के दशक में फ़्रांस में शुरू हुई। इंप्रेशनिस्ट चित्रकार एक पल को पकड़ना चाहते थे: पानी पर झिलमिलाती धूप, रेलगाड़ी से उठती भाप, पोस्त के फूलों से भरे खेत में चलती हवा। वे तेज़ी से, अक्सर खुले में, छोटे और साफ़ दिखने वाले ब्रश के निशानों और बिना मिलाए चटख [[pigment|रंगों]] से पेंट करते थे।

पास से देखो तो इंप्रेशनिस्ट पेंटिंग धब्बों का एक घालमेल लग सकती है। थोड़ा पीछे हटो, तो धब्बे मिलकर झिलमिलाती रोशनी बन जाते हैं। शुरू में आलोचकों को यह बिल्कुल पसंद नहीं आई। आज [[@paris|पेरिस]] से [[@chicago|शिकागो]] तक के संग्रहालयों में इंप्रेशनिस्ट पेंटिंग सबसे लोकप्रिय पेंटिंग में गिनी जाती हैं।

sec.t:
1800 के दशक में कामयाब होने की चाह रखने वाले फ़्रांसीसी कलाकारों को सरकारी सलों में जगह पानी होती थी, जो हर साल लगने वाली एक विशाल प्रदर्शनी थी। इसके निर्णायकों को इतिहास, [[mythology|मिथकों]] और गंभीर व्यक्ति-चित्रों की चिकनी, चमकाई हुई पेंटिंग पसंद थीं। वे नौजवान चित्रकारों के एक समूह को बार-बार ठुकराते रहे, जिनका काम खुरदरा और अधूरा लगता था।

इसलिए 1874 में इस समूह ने पेरिस में अपनी ख़ुद की प्रदर्शनी लगाई। [[@impressionists-monet|क्लोद मोने]] की एक पेंटिंग में भोर के समय का एक बंदरगाह था, नारंगी सूरज और नीले रंग के कुछ फुर्तीले निशानों के साथ। उन्होंने इसका नाम रखा *इंप्रेशन, सनराइज़*, यानी उगते सूरज की छाप। लुई लेरॉय नाम के एक आलोचक ने मज़ाक उड़ाती समीक्षा में इन कलाकारों को "इंप्रेशनिस्ट" कहा, मानो वे बस कच्ची-पक्की पहली छाप ही बना पाते हों। चित्रकारों को यह नाम पसंद आ गया और उन्होंने ख़ुद इसे अपना लिया।

इंप्रेशनिस्टों ने ग़ौर किया कि परछाइयाँ सिर्फ़ स्लेटी या काली नहीं होतीं। बर्फ़ पर परछाइयाँ नीली दिखती हैं, और धूप किसी सफ़ेद दीवार को गुलाबी या सुनहरा कर सकती है। उन्होंने ये रंग बेझिझक पेंट किए।

हर रंग को पैलेट पर मिलाने के बजाय वे अक्सर अलग-अलग रंगों के छोटे-छोटे निशान अगल-बगल रख देते थे। तुम्हारी [[@eyes-see|आँखें]] दूर से उन्हें आपस में घोल लेती हैं, और नतीजा अक्सर मिलाए हुए रंग से ज़्यादा चमकीला लगता है। यही एक वजह है कि इंप्रेशनिस्ट पेंटिंग दमकती-सी लगती हैं।

क्लोद मोने सबसे मशहूर इंप्रेशनिस्ट हैं। जिवर्नी में अपने बगीचे में उन्होंने एक तालाब खुदवाया और ज़िंदगी के आख़िरी दशक कमलिनियों को पेंट करते बिताए, जिनमें से कुछ कई मीटर चौड़े कैनवस पर हैं। पियर-ऑगुस्त रेनुआ ने छन-छनकर आती धूप में नाचती और बतियाती भीड़ पेंट की। एडगर देगा ने मंच के पीछे और अभ्यास करती [[@ballet|बैले नर्तकियों]] को पेंट किया।

औरतें भी इस समूह का हिस्सा थीं। बर्थ मोरिसो ने बगीचे और घर-परिवार की ज़िंदगी पेंट की। पेरिस में बस गईं अमेरिकी चित्रकार मैरी कसाट ने माँओं और बच्चों के चित्र बनाए और इंप्रेशनिज़्म को अमेरिका में लोकप्रिय बनाने में मदद की, जहाँ [[patron|संग्राहकों]] ने बहुत-सी पेंटिंग ख़रीदीं।

1839 में दुनिया के सामने फ़ोटोग्राफ़ी का ऐलान हुआ था। [[@cameras-how|कैमरे]] अब चीज़ों को ठीक वैसे दर्ज कर सकते थे जैसी वे दिखती थीं, इसलिए चित्रकार सोचने लगे कि पेंटिंग ऐसा क्या कर सकती है जो कैमरा नहीं कर सकता। इंप्रेशनिस्टों ने रोशनी, हरकत और भावना पेंट करके इसका जवाब दिया।

उनकी पेंटिंग ने [[@photography-history|तस्वीरों]] से भी कुछ बातें उधार लीं: तस्वीर के किनारे पर कटी हुई आकृतियाँ, या अनोखे कोणों से देखे गए दृश्य। बाद में आए विन्सेंट वैन गॉग जैसे चित्रकारों ने इन विचारों पर आगे काम किया और और आगे गए, और [[@modern-art|आधुनिक कला]] की राह शुरू हो गई।

text: Every time you buy something, even a pencil, you become a consumer. Laws in most countries give consumers certain rights. The product should be safe. The seller should tell the truth about what it is and what it costs. You should be able to choose between products, and if something goes wrong, you should be heard and get a fair fix.

In India, the Consumer Protection Act of 2019 sets out these rights. In the USA, they are spread across several [[federal|federal]] and state laws. In both, shoppers can complain to special bodies without needing an expensive [[@jobs-lawyer|lawyer]].

sec.h: A speech that started a day

sec.t:
In 1965, a young lawyer named Ralph Nader wrote *Unsafe at Any Speed*, arguing that car makers cared more about looks than safety. The book became a bestseller. Within a year, the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]] passed a law setting federal safety standards for cars, and features like [[@seatbelts|seat belts]] became required.

Nader's book showed that one determined consumer could take on huge companies. It also showed that consumer rights are partly about things you never notice, like a toy that doesn't break into sharp pieces. Since 1972, the US Consumer Product Safety Commission has been able to order recalls of dangerous goods, from cots to toys. In a recall, the maker must take the product back, repair it or refund the buyer.

India's first consumer law came in 1986, and was signed on 24 December, now National Consumer Day. The 2019 law updated it for online shopping and misleading adverts, including those by celebrities.

Some rules you can check yourself. Every packet must show its MRP, the maximum price including taxes. Food packets carry a licence number from the food safety regulator, FSSAI, and a list of ingredients. Many electrical goods need a quality mark from the Bureau of Indian Standards. Reading [[@food-labels|food labels]] is one of the easiest ways to use your right to be informed.

If something is faulty, you can first call the National Consumer Helpline on 1915. If that doesn't work, you can file a case at a consumer commission. These exist at district, state and national level, and you can argue your own case.

Online shopping has made some old problems harder. You can't hold the product before you buy it, reviews can be fake, and countdown timers can rush you. Indian rules now require online sellers to show the country of origin, a clear return policy and a way to complain.

Many shoppers also get caught by "sale" prices. A tag that says 50% off a price nobody ever paid is not much of a deal, and knowing your [[@percentages|percentages]] helps. A careful consumer reads the label, keeps the bill and asks questions before paying.

text: Being a chef is hot, fast, tiring and, for people who love it, deeply satisfying. A chef cooks, but also plans menus, orders ingredients, keeps costs down, trains other cooks and makes sure every plate leaving the kitchen is right.

The hours are long. Restaurants are busiest when everyone else is relaxing: evenings, weekends and festivals. A cook may be on their feet for ten hours or more in a kitchen that can feel as hot as a summer afternoon in Nagpur. But many chefs say there is nothing like the rush of a full dining room and a kitchen working well together.

sec.t:
In the late 1800s, a French chef named Auguste Escoffier organised big hotel kitchens like an army. His system, called the brigade, gave each cook one job. At the top is the head chef. Under them is the sous-chef, the second in command. Then come the section cooks, each running one station: sauces, fish, vegetables, grill or pastry.

Many kitchens around the world still use a version of this system. When an order comes in, the person running the pass, the counter where finished food is collected, calls it out. Each station shouts back to show it has heard. It sounds noisy, but it stops mistakes. The head chef tastes sauces, checks how each plate looks and sends back anything that isn't right.

There are many paths. In India, many chefs study at Institutes of Hotel Management after Class 12, getting in through a national entrance exam. In the USA, some go to cooking schools such as the Culinary Institute of America in New York State. Many great cooks never go to college at all. They start as kitchen helpers and learn by watching and doing.

India also has old family traditions of cooking for others, such as the halwais who make sweets and the cooks who prepare grand feasts for weddings. Their skills are often passed from parent to child. A wedding cook in Lucknow or Hyderabad may cook biryani for a thousand guests without ever writing down a recipe.

Not every chef works in a restaurant. Some cook in hospitals, schools, airlines, ships or army camps. The community kitchen at the Golden Temple in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]] serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day, cooked mostly by volunteers in giant pots. Planning food on that scale needs the same skills as running any big kitchen, from getting [[@ratios-cooking|ratios]] right to keeping everyone safe.

Kitchens are full of hazards: hot oil, sharp knives, slippery floors and heavy pots. Good chefs take [[@kitchen-safety|kitchen safety]] seriously and teach it to new cooks from day one. The work is also tiring, and starting pay can be low. Even so, many chefs love the job because cooking is something you can share straight away. You make something with your hands, and a few minutes later you can watch a stranger enjoy it.

text: A grid is a set of lines crossing at right angles, like the squares on graph paper. Put a grid over a map, label the columns with letters and the rows with numbers, and every square gets a short name, like B7. Instead of saying "somewhere near the top, a bit left of the river", you can say "look in B7".

Grids turn a messy question, "where is it?", into a pair of simple labels. The same idea locates a seat in a cinema, a square on a chessboard or a cell in a spreadsheet. On a global scale, lines of latitude and longitude make a grid over the whole planet, and your phone's [[@gps-how|GPS]] uses it to pin you to within a few metres.

sec.h: Along the corridor, up the stairs
sec.t:
Most grids use two labels: one for how far across and one for how far up or down. Teachers often say "along the corridor, then up the stairs" to remember which comes first.

A [[@chess-india|chessboard]] is a perfect grid. Its columns are labelled a to h and its rows 1 to 8, so every square has a name, such as e4. Players can write down whole games this way, and anyone can replay them years later. The board game Battleship works the same way: call out "C5" and hope you hit something.

Some cities are grids themselves. More than 4,000 years ago, the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had main streets crossing at right angles, with blocks of houses between them.

In 1811, planners laid out a grid of numbered streets and avenues across most of Manhattan in [[@new-york|New York]]. That is why a New Yorker can say "meet me at 42nd and 5th" and you know exactly where to go.

India's [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]], planned in the 1950s by the architect Le Corbusier, is divided into rectangular sectors, mostly about 800 metres by 1,200 metres. Each sector is numbered and has its own shops, schools and parks. The number 13 was skipped, apparently because some considered it unlucky.

In 1972, India Post introduced six-digit PIN codes. The first digit stands for a region, and later digits narrow down to a single [[@post-office|post office]] area. A PIN code covers many streets, though, and many Indian homes have no clear address at all.

In 2025, India Post launched DIGIPIN. It lays an invisible grid over the whole country, dividing it into squares about 4 metres by 4 metres. Each square gets a 10-character code worked out from its latitude and longitude. A house in a village with no street name can now share a precise code for deliveries or ambulances.

On a map, each grid square stands for a real area on the ground. If the map's [[@maps-scale|scale]] says each square is 1 kilometre across, you can count squares to estimate distances. Hikers, soldiers and rescue teams use grid references to tell each other exactly where to go, often down to a few metres.

It all comes back to one simple trick. Draw lines, label them, and a whole world of places becomes something you can name, share and find.

text: Music is full of patterns, and patterns are what maths describes. Every musical note is a [[vibration|vibration]] with a [[frequency|frequency]], a number of shakes per second. Notes that sound good together usually have frequencies in simple ratios, like 2 to 1 or 3 to 2.

[[@maths-music-rhythm|Rhythm is maths too]]. Beats are counted, grouped and divided, like fractions. A tabla player landing perfectly on the first beat after a long, tricky phrase is doing a kind of calculation, even if it feels like pure music. People have noticed these links for at least 2,500 years, in Greece, India, China and elsewhere.

st.reveal: Half the string vibrates twice as fast, so the frequency doubles. Our ears hear doubled frequencies as "the same note, higher". That jump is called an octave, and it is the basis of almost every musical scale.

sec.t:
An old story says that the Greek thinker [[@pythagoras|Pythagoras]] noticed that strings of certain lengths sounded good together. Whether or not he did it himself, his followers studied the numbers.

They found that if one string is exactly half the length of another, it plays the same note, but higher. Today we call that an [[octave|octave]]. A string two-thirds as long plays a note called a fifth, which sounds very harmonious with the first. Three-quarters gives a fourth. The simpler the ratio, the smoother the two notes sound together.

Modern science explains why. Halving a string doubles its frequency. The A note that orchestras tune to vibrates 440 times a second, and the A one octave higher vibrates 880 times. Your [[@ears-hear|ears]] hear these doublings as the same note at a different height.

Indian classical music has detailed [[rhythm|rhythm]] cycles called *tala*. Teentaal, common in Hindustani music, has 16 beats split into four groups of four. Adi tala, common in Carnatic music, has 8 beats grouped 4 + 2 + 2.

Players love rhythmic puzzles. A *tihai* is a phrase repeated three times so that it ends exactly on *sam*, the first beat of the cycle. To make it land, a [[@tabla|tabla]] player must work out the length of the phrase and the gaps so that three copies fit perfectly. Audiences often clap when the last stroke hits sam.

[[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poetry uses short and long [[syllable|syllables]]. A long one takes twice the time of a short one. Scholars asked: how many different rhythms can fill a line of a given length? The answers are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and so on, with each number the sum of the two before.

Indian scholars such as Virahanka, perhaps in the 7th century, and Hemachandra, around 1150, described this pattern. In Europe it is named after Fibonacci, who wrote about it in 1202 in a puzzle about rabbits. The same numbers turn up in pine cones and [[@fibonacci-nature|sunflowers]].

बहुत-से लोग अस्पताल में पहली बार इमरजेंसी विभाग से दाख़िल होते हैं। भारत में इसे "कैज़ुअल्टी" भी कहते हैं और अमेरिका में "ईआर"। यहाँ एक नर्स ट्रायज करती है। यह शब्द फ़्रांसीसी *trier* से आया है, जिसका मतलब है छाँटना। हर मरीज़ को जल्दी से जाँचा जाता है और इस हिसाब से छाँटा जाता है कि उसकी परेशानी कितनी फ़ौरी है।

सबसे गंभीर मरीज़ों को एम्बुलेंस लाती है। हो सकता है रेडियो पर ख़बर मिलते ही एक टीम पहले से इंतज़ार कर रही हो। बाकी लोगों को ज़्यादा देर रुकना पड़ सकता है। यह नाइंसाफ़ी लग सकती है, पर असल में इसका मतलब है कि व्यवस्था ठीक काम कर रही है।

सर्जरी ऑपरेशन थिएटर में होती है, जिसे बेहद साफ़ रखा जाता है। सर्जन [[@how-hand-sanitiser|अपने हाथ और बाँहें रगड़-रगड़कर धोते हैं]], फिर कीटाणु-रहित गाउन, दस्ताने और मास्क पहनते हैं। औज़ारों को गर्मी और भाप से साफ़ किया जाता है ताकि कोई कीटाणु ज़िंदा न बचे।

यह सावधानी काफ़ी नई है। 1847 में वियना के एक डॉक्टर इग्नाज़ ज़ेमेलवाइस ने देखा कि जब डॉक्टर [[@body-handwashing-history|क्लोरीन के घोल से हाथ धोते]] थे, तो बच्चे को जन्म देने के बाद बहुत कम माँओं की मौत होती थी। शुरू में कई डॉक्टरों ने उनकी बात अनसुनी कर दी। आज [[@soap-germs|साबुन]] से हाथ धोना हर अस्पताल के सबसे ज़रूरी नियमों में से एक है।

इलाज की जगहें बहुत पुरानी हैं। [[emperor|सम्राट]] [[@ashoka|अशोक]] ने ईसा पूर्व तीसरी सदी में भारत के बड़े हिस्से पर राज किया। उन्होंने पत्थर पर लिखवाया कि उन्होंने इंसानों और जानवरों के इलाज का इंतज़ाम किया है। 800 से भी ज़्यादा साल पहले बग़दाद, दमिश्क और काहिरा जैसे शहरों में बड़े-बड़े अस्पताल बने, जिनमें अलग-अलग वार्ड और पुस्तकालय भी थे।

1850 के दशक में क्रीमिया के युद्ध के दौरान ब्रिटिश नर्स फ़्लोरेंस नाइटिंगेल ने तुर्की के एक गंदे फ़ौजी अस्पताल की सफ़ाई करवाई, और वार्डों को हवादार और साफ़ रखने के लिए लड़ीं। बाद में उन्होंने लंदन में नर्सों के लिए एक स्कूल खोला और नर्सिंग को इज़्ज़तदार, सीखा-सिखाया पेशा बना दिया।

अमेरिका में बेंजामिन फ़्रैंकलिन और डॉ. थॉमस बॉन्ड ने 1751 में फ़िलाडेल्फ़िया में पेंसिल्वेनिया हॉस्पिटल शुरू किया, जो वहाँ के उपनिवेशों का पहला अस्पताल था। 1956 में भारत ने नई दिल्ली में अखिल भारतीय आयुर्विज्ञान संस्थान (एम्स) खोला, जहाँ आज भी हर रोज़ हज़ारों मरीज़ों का इलाज होता है।

सबसे गंभीर मरीज़ इंटेंसिव केयर यूनिट यानी आईसीयू में जाते हैं। यहाँ हर मरीज़ के पास कई मशीनें होती हैं: दिल की धड़कन और [[oxygen|ऑक्सीजन]] का स्तर दिखाते बीप-बीप करते मॉनिटर, बूँद-बूँद दवा और पानी चढ़ाने वाली ड्रिप, और साँस लेने में मदद करने वाले वेंटिलेटर। यहाँ एक नर्स शायद सिर्फ़ एक या दो मरीज़ों की देखभाल करती है।

इतने तारों और स्क्रीनों के बीच यह डरावना लग सकता है। पर हर बीप का मतलब है कि कोई चौकसी कर रहा है।

text: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French general who rose to power after the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]] and crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804. Born in 1769 on the island of Corsica, he became one of the most successful military commanders in history, conquering much of Europe.

He also changed how France was governed. His Napoleonic Code set out laws that treated citizens more equally, and it shaped legal systems in many countries. But his wars cost millions of lives. sec.t:
Napoleon was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, a year after France took over the island from Genoa. His first language was Corsican, a [[dialect|dialect]] close to Italian, and he spoke French with an accent all his life.

He trained as an artillery officer. In 1793, aged 24, he helped recapture the port of Toulon from British forces, and was quickly promoted. In 1796 he led a French army into Italy and won battle after battle. In 1798 he invaded Egypt, bringing more than a hundred scientists and scholars with him. In 1799 his soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, the key that later let scholars read Egyptian [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]].

In 1803, needing money for war with Britain, Napoleon sold France's vast Louisiana Territory to the United States for 15 million dollars. It stretched from the [[@mississippi|Mississippi river]] to the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]].

The [[@usa-statehood|Louisiana Purchase]] roughly doubled the size of the United States. Parts of 15 present-day states came from it. Today, the state of Louisiana still bases its civil law on French traditions, and the city of [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]] keeps French street names and food.

By 1810 Napoleon controlled or dominated much of Europe, from Spain to Poland. Only Britain, protected by its navy, held out. Napoleon also looked further east. In 1799 he wrote to [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] of Mysore, promising help against the British in India.

In 1812 he invaded Russia with an army of around half a million men or more. The Russians retreated, burning crops and villages as they went. Napoleon reached Moscow, but it was largely burned and empty. Forced to retreat through a freezing winter, his army was destroyed by cold, hunger and attacks. Only a small fraction of his soldiers came back.

In 1814 his enemies captured Paris and exiled him to the small Mediterranean island of Elba. Within a year he escaped, returned to France, and took power again for about a hundred days.

On 18 June 1815, at Waterloo in today's Belgium, he was defeated by a British-led army under the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Blücher. This time the British sent him to St Helena, a tiny island in the South Atlantic, about 1,900 kilometres from Africa. He died there in 1821. His tomb now lies under the golden dome of Les Invalides in Paris.

sec.t:
पुराने भारतीय राजाओं की ताकत कुछ हद तक उनके हाथियों से आँकी जाती थी। [[@chanakya|चाणक्य]] से जुड़ी राज चलाने की किताब *अर्थशास्त्र* में हाथियों के लिए एक पूरे सरकारी विभाग का ब्यौरा है। उसमें लिखा है कि हाथियों को कैसे पकड़ा जाए, क्या खिलाया जाए, कैसे सधाया जाए और उनकी सेहत का ध्यान कैसे रखा जाए। वह हाथियों के जंगलों की हिफ़ाज़त की बात भी करती है।

सिकंदर का सामना युद्ध के हाथियों से 326 ईसा पूर्व में भारत में हाइडस्पीज़ नदी पर हुआ, जिसे आज झेलम कहते हैं। राजा पोरस के पास शायद 85 से 200 हाथी थे। गिनती इस पर निर्भर है कि तुम किस पुराने लेखक की बात मानते हो। सिकंदर जीत गया, पर उसके घोड़े बिदक गए और सैनिकों के हौसले हिल गए। कुछ ही समय बाद उसकी सेना ने [[@alexander-india|भारत]] में और आगे बढ़ने से इनकार कर दिया।

लगभग 303 ईसा पूर्व में [[@mauryan-empire|मौर्य साम्राज्य]] के संस्थापक चंद्रगुप्त मौर्य ने यूनानी राजा सेल्यूकस से एक सौदा किया। सेल्यूकस ने वह ज़मीन छोड़ दी जो आज अफ़ग़ानिस्तान और पाकिस्तान में है। बदले में उसे लगभग 500 हाथी मिले।

दो साल बाद तुर्की में इप्सस की लड़ाई में इन्हीं हाथियों की मदद से सेल्यूकस जीता। यानी भारतीय हाथियों ने भारत से बहुत दूर एक युद्ध का फ़ैसला करने में हाथ बँटाया।

हाथी हाथियों से भी लड़े। 217 ईसा पूर्व में दो यूनानी राजाओं के बीच रफ़िया की लड़ाई में अफ़्रीकी जंगली हाथियों का सामना भारतीय हाथियों से हुआ। इतिहासकार पॉलिबियस के अनुसार अफ़्रीकी हाथी, जो छोटे थे, घबराकर भाग खड़े हुए। पुराने युद्धों में इस्तेमाल हुए उत्तरी अफ़्रीका के ये जंगली हाथी अब [[extinct|विलुप्त]] हो चुके हैं।

{{story:people-mahouts}}

सबसे मशहूर युद्ध-हाथी उत्तरी अफ़्रीका के [[@carthage|कार्थेज]] के सेनापति हैनिबल के साथ चले। 218 ईसा पूर्व में वह लगभग 37 हाथियों वाली सेना लेकर स्पेन से बर्फ़ीले आल्प्स पहाड़ पार करके रोम पर हमला करने निकला। पहाड़ी दर्रे तंग और बर्फ़ से फिसलन भरे थे। साल-डेढ़ साल में लगभग सारे हाथी मर गए, पर उनकी कहानी अमर हो गई।

रोमनों का हाथियों से पहला सामना कुछ साल पहले, 280 ईसा पूर्व में, राजा पिर्रस के खिलाफ़ हुआ था। जल्द ही उन्होंने तरकीबें सीख लीं। सैनिक एक तरफ़ हट जाते, हाथियों को खाली जगह से निकल जाने देते और फिर पीछे से हमला करते। कुछ लेखक कहते हैं कि सेनाएँ हाथियों को डराने के लिए चीखते सूअरों का इस्तेमाल करती थीं, क्योंकि हाथियों को वह आवाज़ बिल्कुल पसंद नहीं थी।

भारत में हाथी लगभग 2,000 साल और सेनाओं में बने रहे। राजपूत, मुग़ल और दक्कन के शासक हज़ारों हाथी रखते थे। बादशाह हाथी पर सवार होकर लड़ाई में उतरते ताकि उनके सैनिक उन्हें देख सकें, हालाँकि इससे राजा आसान निशाना भी बन जाता था। हाथी चलती-फिरती कमान चौकी भी थे। हाथी की ऊँची पीठ से सेनापति पूरा मैदान देख सकता था, और उसके सैनिक उसे। पर अगर हाथी मुड़कर भाग जाता, तो सेना अक्सर मान लेती कि लड़ाई हार गए।

1526 में पानीपत की पहली लड़ाई में बाबर की बंदूकों और तोपों ने इब्राहिम लोदी के हाथियों को डरा दिया, और कुछ हाथी मुड़कर लोदी की अपनी ही सेना को रौंदते हुए भागे। जैसे-जैसे बारूद फैला, हाथियों पर निशाना लगाना बहुत आसान हो गया।

लड़ाई में धावा बोलना बंद करने के बहुत बाद तक हाथी सेनाओं के लिए काम करते रहे। ब्रिटिश भारत में वे भारी तोपें खींचते थे, और दूसरे विश्व युद्ध में बर्मा के घने जंगलों में, जहाँ ट्रक नहीं जा सकते थे, सामान ढोते थे।

हाथी समझदार होते हैं और लोगों को बरसों याद रखते हैं। आज भारत के हाथी कानून से सुरक्षित हैं, और उनके साथ काम करने का हुनर उन [[@people-mahouts|महावतों]] के पास ज़िंदा है जो मंदिरों और जंगलों के हाथियों की देखभाल करते हैं। ये जानवर इतनी गहरी गड़गड़ाहट से आपस में बात करते हैं कि इंसान उसे सुन ही नहीं पाते। यह [[@elephants-talk|हाथियों की बातचीत]] की अपनी अलग कहानी है।

text: In the hot months, the plains of north India can reach 45°C. For British officials and soldiers raised in cool, rainy Britain, that heat felt unbearable. Many also fell ill and died from diseases like malaria and cholera. So, from the 1820s onwards, they built small towns high in the hills, where the air was cooler.

These "hill stations" became summer homes, hospitals, schools and holiday spots. The biggest of them, Shimla in [[@himachal|Himachal]], became the summer capital of British India from 1864. For several months a year, the people ruling one-sixth of humanity did it from a mountain ridge.

sec.t:
The trick is height. Air gets thinner and colder as you climb, by roughly 6.5°C for every 1,000 m. Shimla sits about 2,200 m up, so it is often around 14°C cooler than Delhi. Ooty in the Nilgiris and Darjeeling in the eastern Himalaya are at similar heights.

Before the railways, moving the government was a giant chore. Files, furniture, pianos and officials travelled up by bullock cart, pony, palanquin and the backs of porters. Later, tiny [[@india-wonder-toy-train|mountain trains]] zigzagged up the slopes and made the trip far easier.

Shimla's grandest building, the Viceregal Lodge, was finished in 1888. It had electric lights from the start, a rare luxury anywhere in 1888. After independence it became a research institute, and today visitors can walk the same wooden corridors where viceroys once decided the fate of millions.

sec.h: A little England in the clouds
sec.t:
Homesickness shaped these towns as much as heat. The British built cottages with English names, stone churches and a long street called the Mall for evening walks. Boarding schools opened so children didn't have to be shipped to Britain, such as the Lawrence School at Sanawar in 1847.

In Darjeeling, a doctor named Archibald Campbell planted tea seeds in 1841. The hills turned out to be perfect for it, and Darjeeling [[@tea|tea]] became one of the most prized in the world.

Escaping the summer was not a British invention. The Mughal emperor Jahangir loved spending summers in the cool valleys of Kashmir, two centuries earlier. Indian rulers had their own hill palaces too.

The idea also travelled. Kodaikanal in Tamil Nadu was started in 1845 by American missionaries looking to escape the plains. In the early 1900s, Americans ruling the Philippines built the hill town of Baguio as their own summer capital, inspired by the British hill stations of India.

After 1947, hill stations became holiday towns for Indian families. Shimla, Mussoorie, Ooty, Munnar and Mount Abu now fill with tourists every summer. Matheran, near Mumbai, still bans cars, so visitors walk, ride horses or take a hand-pulled rickshaw.

Popularity has a price. Towns designed for a few thousand people now host many times that, and Shimla ran desperately short of water in 2018. Some writers still find peace there, though. [[@ruskin-bond|Ruskin Bond]] has lived in Landour above Mussoorie for decades, and the quiet hills fill his stories. Your body notices those heights too, in ways explained by the science of [[@altitude|altitude]].

text: Mysuru Dasara is a ten-day festival in the city of Mysuru, in Karnataka, held during Navaratri in September or October. It celebrates the victory of good over evil, and especially the goddess Chamundeshwari, who, according to legend, defeated the buffalo-headed demon Mahishasura on the hill above the city. The name Mysuru is often linked to him.

Over the ten days, the city fills with music, dance, [[@wrestling-india|wrestling]], food fairs and flower shows. Mysuru Palace glows each evening with nearly a lakh light bulbs. The festival ends on Vijayadashami with the Jamboo Savari, a grand procession led by an elephant carrying a golden howdah with an idol of the goddess.

The festival falls in the same season across India, but traditions differ. In north India, many people burn effigies of Ravana, while in Kolkata the focus is Durga Puja. Mysuru celebrates with a royal procession honouring the goddess Chamundeshwari.

sec.t:
Dasara in Mysuru goes back to the kings of the [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] [[empire|empire]], who held an enormous autumn festival with processions, music and elephants. Visitors from Portugal and Persia wrote about it in wonder.

After Vijayanagara fell, the Wodeyar kings of Mysore carried the tradition on. Raja Wodeyar I is said to have begun celebrating it in 1610. The festival continued under later rulers, and the Wodeyar family still performs private royal [[ritual|rituals]] in the palace. Since India's independence, the state government has organised the public festival, and it is Karnataka's official state festival, the Nadahabba.

The final day brings the Jamboo Savari. Weeks before, trained elephants walk in from forest camps in Karnataka with their [[@people-mahouts|mahouts]], the people who look after and guide them. They practise walking through traffic, crowds and loud bands, so they stay calm on the day.

On Vijayadashami, the lead elephant carries a golden howdah, a seat weighing about 750 kg, with an idol of Chamundeshwari. Decorated elephants, horses, bands, dancers and colourful floats from districts across the state follow it about 5 km from the palace to the Bannimantap grounds. In the evening, a torchlight parade ends the festival.

Some animal welfare groups have raised concerns about the stress on elephants from crowds and noise. Organisers say the animals are carefully trained and checked by vets. The debate is part of a wider conversation in India about how temple and festival elephants should be treated.

Mysuru is known for much more than Dasara. Its rulers in the 1700s included Hyder Ali and his son [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]], whose capital was at nearby Srirangapatna. Mysore pak, a rich sweet made from gram flour, ghee and sugar, is said to have been invented in the palace kitchen.

The city is also famous for Mysore [[@silk|silk]] saris with gold borders, for sandalwood soap and incense, and for Mysore paintings with gold leaf. On Chamundi Hill above the city, a huge statue of Mahishasura greets visitors climbing up to the goddess's temple, as if he is still waiting for the next round.

text: The Sydney Opera House sits on a point of land sticking into Sydney Harbour in Australia. In 1957, a young Danish architect named Jørn Utzon won a competition to design it. His drawings showed a cluster of white shells, but no one, including Utzon, knew how to build them.

Work began in 1959. It took years of experiments, early computers, a bitter quarrel and a change of architect before the building opened on 20 October 1973. Today its shells are as famous a symbol of Australia as the kangaroo, and it hosts concerts, opera, ballet and plays almost every day of the year.

st.prompt: For years nobody could work out how to build the Opera House's curved roof shells. What idea finally solved it?

options.t: Making every shell from parts of one big sphere
Blowing up giant balloons and pouring concrete over them
Bending sheets of steel by hand on site

st.reveal: Utzon realised that if every curve came from the same sphere, the concrete pieces could be made in identical moulds. The shells became sets of ribs, cast on the ground and lifted into place by crane. A wooden model of the sphere showing this is still displayed at the building.

myth: The Opera House roof is painted white.

The roof is covered in just over a million tiles made in Sweden, in two shades, glossy white and matt cream. They are arranged in a chevron pattern, and their smooth glaze lets the rain wash them clean.
facts: about 102 million Australian dollars, against an early estimate of 7 million

sec.t:
The New South Wales government held an open competition in 1956, and more than 200 architects entered. Utzon's design was more a sketch of an idea than a plan. It had huge curved roofs rising over two halls, all resting on a heavy stone platform.

The builders started on the platform before the roof was designed. That was a mistake. When the roof was finally worked out, it was so heavy that parts of the platform had to be pulled down and rebuilt with stronger columns.

The shells are covered in just over a million ceramic tiles, made in Sweden and fitted in big panels. There are two kinds: shiny white and matt cream. Together they make the roof glow in sunshine and look softer on cloudy days.

The tallest shell reaches about 67 m above the harbour, roughly as high as a 22-storey building. The building rests on hundreds of concrete piers sunk into the harbour floor.

Under the largest shells is the Concert Hall, which seats more than 2,500 people. Its grand organ has about 10,000 pipes, and it took ten years to build. The smaller hall next door is used for opera and ballet, and there are several smaller theatres tucked underneath.

sec.h: The architect who never saw it
sec.t:
As costs rose, a new state government cut off Utzon's payments and argued over his plans for the inside. In 1966 he resigned and left Australia. He never returned. A team of Australian architects finished the interiors, which ended up quite different from his designs.

Most of the money came from a special state lottery, so taxpayers paid relatively little. The final bill was about 102 million Australian dollars, nearly fifteen times the first estimate.

Utzon lived to see his work honoured. In 2003 he won the Pritzker Prize, the top award in [[architecture|architecture]], and in 2007 the Opera House became a World Heritage Site. He died the next year, in Denmark, having seen photographs of his finished building but never the real thing. Many visitors who come for an [[@opera|opera]] or a ballet now walk first to the edge of the harbour to look up at the shells he imagined.

text: A speech becomes famous when it says something important at exactly the right moment, in words simple enough to remember. The best speeches are often short. They use plain words, repeat a key line, tell a small story and end with a strong picture in the listener's mind.

The moment matters as much as the words. Jawaharlal Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was given at midnight as India became independent. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" was spoken to a quarter of a million people who had marched for equal rights. People remembered the words because they remembered the day.

st.prompt: How long did Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address last?

options.t: About two minutes
About twenty minutes
About two hours

st.reveal: It had only about 270 words. The main speaker that day, Edward Everett, spoke for about two hours. Everett later wrote to Lincoln that Lincoln had said more in two minutes than he had in two hours.

d.try: Write a one-minute speech about something you care about, like a school rule or a favourite animal. Use one short line that you repeat three times, and end on your strongest sentence. Say it to your family and ask which line they remember an hour later.
myth: Great speakers are born that way and don't need practice.
Most famous speakers practised hard and rewrote their speeches many times. Gandhi was so shy as a young lawyer in Bombay that he could not get through his first case in court.
facts: 1893, opened with "Sisters and brothers of America"

sec.t:
In November 1863, in the middle of the [[@us-civil-war|American Civil War]], a cemetery for soldiers opened at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The main speaker, Edward Everett, spoke for about two hours. Then [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] stood up and spoke about 270 words.

He said the country had been "conceived in liberty", and that the living must make sure the dead had not died in vain. Some newspapers thought it was too short. Today it is carved in stone at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington DC, and American children learn it by heart.

Just before midnight on 14 August 1947, Nehru spoke to the [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] in Delhi. "Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny," he said, and "at the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom."

A tryst is a promise to meet. The idea that a whole nation had kept an appointment with its future was easy to picture. Five years earlier, Gandhi had given a very different kind of speech, launching the [[@quit-india|Quit India movement]] with just three words for his followers: "Do or die."

On 28 August 1963, [[@martin-luther-king|Martin Luther King Jr.]] spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Near the end, the gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out, "Tell them about the dream, Martin." He put aside his notes. Again and again he repeated "I have a dream", each time painting a picture of a fairer America.

That repetition is an old trick. It gives listeners a beat to hold on to, like the chorus of a song. King was a preacher, and he had used parts of the dream passage in earlier sermons and speeches, so the words came easily when he needed them.

Famous speeches usually do a few things well. They speak to a big moment. They use words a child could follow. They repeat a line until it sticks. And they are spoken by someone the audience trusts.

[[@radio-invented|Radio]], television and now phones let a speech travel far beyond the room. In 2013 Malala Yousafzai, aged 16, spoke at the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] about every child's right to go to school. Millions watched online, and her words were shared in classrooms on both sides of the world.

text: Inside an apple's cells, two things are kept in separate compartments: an [[enzyme|enzyme]] called polyphenol oxidase and natural chemicals called polyphenols. When you cut or bite an apple, you break open millions of cells and the two meet. With oxygen from the air, the enzyme turns the polyphenols into new chemicals that link up into brown [[pigment|pigments]], related to the [[melanin|melanin]] in your skin.
That brown layer may help protect the fruit. In nature, it may slow down insects and germs at a wound, a little like a scab. For us, it's just a sign that air has been at work.

st.prompt: You cut three apple slices. Which one stays white the longest?

options.t: The one brushed with lemon juice
The one left in a warm, sunny spot
The one rubbed with a little sugar

st.reveal: Lemon juice is acidic, and acid slows the browning enzyme. It also contains vitamin C, which reacts with oxygen before the apple's own chemicals can. Warmth speeds browning up.

myth: A brown apple slice has gone bad and shouldn't be eaten.
Browning is a harmless chemical reaction, not rot. The slice may taste a little different, but it is safe. Rot is caused by moulds and bacteria and smells and looks quite different.
facts: the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia

sec.t:
Anything that blocks the enzyme or the oxygen slows [[@food-science-apples-brown|browning]]. [[@citrus|Lemon juice]] is acidic, and the enzyme works poorly in [[acid|acid]]. Lemon also contains [[vitamin|vitamin]] C, which grabs oxygen first.

Cold slows the enzyme too, which is why fruit salad keeps better in the fridge. Dunking slices in water keeps air away for a while. Cooking destroys the enzyme altogether, so stewed apple doesn't keep darkening. The same reaction turns cut potatoes, bananas and brinjal brown.

Browning is a kind of [[oxidation|oxidation]], a reaction with oxygen. It's related to the way iron turns into orange flakes when left out in damp air, which you can read about in [[@rust|rust]]. Both happen faster when it's warm.

In 2015, the US Department of Agriculture approved a genetically modified apple called the Arctic apple. Scientists had switched off the [[gene|genes]] for the browning enzyme, so its cut slices stay pale. Some people welcome less waste, while others prefer not to eat genetically modified food.

The wild ancestors of today's apples still grow in the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and western [[@china-today|China]]. Forests of wild apple trees there have fruit of many shapes, colours and tastes. The name of Kazakhstan's biggest city, Almaty, is often linked to the Kazakh word for apple.

Traders and travellers along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] carried apples east and west. The Romans spread them across Europe, and European settlers brought them to North America.

India's apples grow mainly in the cool hills of Jammu and [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] and [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]]. In 1916, an American named Samuel Evans Stokes, who had settled in Himachal, brought saplings of Red Delicious and other kinds from the USA to Kotgarh. Apple growing spread across the hills and changed the lives of many farming families.

In the USA, Washington State grows the most apples by far. In both countries, apples bruised on the way to market are often wasted, though they can still make good juice, jam or chutney, as you can read in [[@food-waste|food waste]].

text: Tamarind is the fruit of a large, shady tree. Its curved brown pods hold a sticky, dark pulp around shiny seeds. The pulp is sour, a little sweet and very tangy, and cooks across India use it to give food a sharp, fruity sourness.

It goes into sambar and rasam in the south, into the sweet-sour chutney served with samosas and [[@chaat|chaat]] in the north, and into the spicy water of [[@pani-puri|pani puri]]. Thai, Mexican, Caribbean and many African kitchens use it too. Tamarind trees probably came from Africa long ago, but India now grows more tamarind than any other country.

st.prompt: The word "tamarind" comes from Arabic. What does it mean?

options.t: Date of India
Sour fruit
Brown bean

st.reveal: Arab traders called it tamar hindi, "Indian date", because its sticky brown pulp looked like dates and they bought it in India. The tree itself probably came from Africa.

d.try: Ask an adult for a small piece of tamarind and a dull copper or brass coin or object. Rub a little tamarind pulp onto half of it with a cloth, wait a few minutes, then rinse and dry it. Compare the two halves. The acid in tamarind dissolves the dark layer on the metal.
myth: Tamarind must be an Indian plant, since its scientific name is "indica".
The name records where Europeans and Arabs met it, not where it began. Most botanists think the tree is originally from tropical Africa and reached India in ancient times.
facts: Name comes from Arabic tamar hindi, meaning date of India
tartaric acid, also found in grapes

sec.t:
The tamarind tree belongs to the [[legume|legume]] family, the same family as peas, beans and peanuts. Its pods are a kind of bean pod, but instead of soft green beans, they're filled with brown pulp held together by tough threads.

Like many plants in the pea family, the tree has feathery leaves made of tiny leaflets that fold up at night. It can grow taller than a three-storey building and live for well over a century. In parts of South India, old tamarind trees line village roads, and families have harvested the same trees for generations.

Tamarind wood is very hard. The seeds, once roasted, can be eaten, and a powder made from them is used in factories to stiffen cotton and jute threads.

sec.h: From Africa to the Indian kitchen

sec.t:
Tamarind's sourness comes mainly from tartaric [[acid|acid]], the same acid found in grapes. The pulp also holds a lot of natural sugar, so ripe tamarind tastes sweet and sour at once. Cooks balance it with jaggery, salt and chilli. Unripe green pods are much sharper and are pickled or ground into chutneys.

In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, tamarind rice, called *puliyogare* or *puli sadam*, is a favourite for journeys and temple offerings, because the sourness helps it keep for longer. Many [[@south-indian-meals|South Indian meals]] rely on it. Cooks soak a lump of pulp in warm water, then squeeze it to make the thin, sour liquid that goes into rasam. Worcestershire sauce, the dark sauce from England, has tamarind in it too.

sec.h: A cleaner as well as a food
sec.t:
The same acid that makes tamarind sour can clean metal. Copper and brass slowly darken as they react with air, forming a dull layer on top, a cousin of [[@rust|rust]]. Rubbing them with tamarind pulp [[dissolve|dissolves]] that layer and brings back the shine. In many Indian homes and temples, brass lamps and pooja vessels are still cleaned this way.

Tamarind trees also feature in folk tales. In some parts of South India, people say ghosts live in them and warn children not to sleep beneath one at night. Scientists would say that's only a story. For many children, though, the best part of a tamarind tree is simpler: a fresh, sour pod, a pinch of salt and chilli, and a face screwed up in delight.
